directAnswer: Pope Clement IV was Guy Foulques of Saint-Gilles in southern France, a lawyer and former married layman who became a priest after his wife's death and reigned from 5 February 1265 to 29 November 1268. His pontificate saw Charles of Anjou conquer the Kingdom of Sicily with papal backing, and he is also remembered for requesting the scientific writings of Roger Bacon.

paras: Guy Foulques was born at Saint-Gilles, near the mouth of the Rhône. He trained in law and became a respected jurist and adviser in the service of King Louis IX of France. He married and had children, among them daughters. After his wife died, he entered the clergy.

His rise in the Church was rapid. He became bishop of Le Puy, then archbishop of Narbonne, and Urban IV created him cardinal bishop of Sabina. When Urban died in 1264, Guy was away on a legation connected with the civil strife in England between Henry III and his barons. The cardinals, meeting at Perugia, elected him in his absence, and he accepted after returning to Italy.

Clement completed the policy Urban IV had begun. Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX, received the Kingdom of Sicily as a papal fief and was crowned in Rome in January 1266 by cardinals acting for the pope. A month later Charles defeated and killed Manfred at the Battle of Benevento.

In 1268 the young Conradin, the last legitimate Hohenstaufen heir, invaded Italy to recover his inheritance. Clement excommunicated him. Charles defeated Conradin at Tagliacozzo and had him executed at Naples in October 1268, a few weeks before Clement's own death. The episode tied the papacy closely to the house of Anjou for decades.

sections.h2: Roger Bacon and the Opus Maius
paras: Before his election, Guy had learned of the English Franciscan Roger Bacon and his ambitious ideas for reforming learning through languages, mathematics, optics and experimental science. As pope he wrote to Bacon asking him to send his work, despite the restrictions Bacon's order placed on publishing. Bacon responded by composing the Opus maius, along with shorter companion works, and sent them to Clement around 1267.
There is no record of how Clement received them, and he died soon after. Still, the exchange is one of the best known links between a medieval pope and the history of science.

sections.h2: Papal Provisions and a Restrained Household
paras: As a canonist, Clement issued the decretal Licet ecclesiarum in 1265, asserting the pope's right to dispose of all church benefices and reserving to the Holy See those that fell vacant while their holders were at the papal court. Later popes built extensively on this principle.

Contemporaries noted that he avoided enriching his relatives, unusual for his time. He spent his pontificate at Perugia and Viterbo and died at Viterbo on 29 November 1268. The disagreements among the cardinals that followed produced a vacancy of nearly three years, the longest in papal history.

keyFacts: Born Guy Foulques at Saint-Gilles, France; a married lawyer before ordination
Archbishop of Narbonne and cardinal bishop of Sabina
Backed Charles of Anjou, who defeated Manfred (1266) and Conradin (1268)
Requested Roger Bacon's writings, prompting the Opus maius
Issued the decretal Licet ecclesiarum on papal provisions (1265)

faqs.question: Was Pope Clement IV married?
faqs.answer: Yes. Before ordination Guy Foulques was a married layman and lawyer with children. He became a cleric after his wife died, which was permitted, and later rose to archbishop, cardinal and pope.

faqs.question: What was Clement IV's connection to Roger Bacon?
faqs.answer: Clement asked the Franciscan scholar to send him his writings. Bacon answered with the Opus maius and related works, which he sent to the pope around 1267.

faqs.question: What happened after Clement IV died?
faqs.answer: The cardinals at Viterbo were divided for almost three years, from late 1268 to 1271. That vacancy ended with the election of Gregory X, who then issued new rules for conclaves.
